title: Sensory Reception
purpose: Codex-ready authored formative bank. Source quizzes and textbook review were used for scope/difficulty calibration; these are fresh practice items rather than a learner-facing answer-key dump.

lessons.label: Eye structures and the path of light
Retina, rods, cones and visual interpretation
Pitch, loudness, hearing impairment and technology

concepts.definition: detection of a stimulus by a specialized sensory receptor
concepts.scenario: Warmth activates temperature receptors in the skin before the brain interprets the experience.
concepts.misconception: Sensory reception and perception are the same event in the same location.
concepts.cue: Focus on the first event: detecting the stimulus.
concepts.explanation: Reception is detection at the receptor. Sensation and perception require CNS processing.

concepts.definition: sensation occurs when sensory impulses reach the cerebral cortex; perception is the brain's interpretation of that information
concepts.scenario: Two witnesses receive similar visual input but interpret details differently.
concepts.misconception: The eye itself creates the conscious visual perception.
concepts.cue: Ask where meaning is assigned to sensory information.
concepts.explanation: Receptors detect and transduce; the brain produces conscious sensation and interpretation.

concepts.definition: reduced awareness of constant, unimportant sensory input
concepts.scenario: After several minutes you stop noticing the pressure of clothing on your skin.
concepts.misconception: Adaptation means the receptor has permanently stopped working.
concepts.cue: Look for decreasing awareness of an unchanged stimulus.
concepts.explanation: Adaptation reduces attention to constant input while preserving sensitivity to meaningful change.

concepts.definition: photoreceptors detect light, chemoreceptors detect chemicals, mechanoreceptors detect mechanical forces, and thermoreceptors detect temperature
concepts.scenario: Hair cells bend in the inner ear when fluid or sound-driven structures move.
concepts.misconception: All sensory receptors detect the same form of energy and the brain decides the type later.
concepts.cue: Match receptor type to the form of stimulus energy.
concepts.explanation: Different receptors are specialized to transduce different stimulus types into neural information.

concepts.term: path of light through the eye
concepts.definition: light passes through the cornea, aqueous humour, pupil, lens and vitreous humour before reaching the retina
concepts.scenario: A ray entering the eye is bent mainly by the cornea and then fine-focused by the lens onto the retina.
concepts.misconception: The optic nerve carries incoming light to the retina.
concepts.cue: Trace actual light, not the neural signal.
concepts.explanation: Light reaches the retina first; neural information leaves the eye through the optic nerve afterward.
sourceRefs: Teacher slides: Anatomy of the Eye & Vision

concepts.definition: sclera protects, choroid absorbs stray light and nourishes, iris controls pupil size, lens focuses, retina contains photoreceptors, and optic nerve carries neural output
concepts.scenario: Damage to the optic nerve can prevent visual information from reaching the brain even if the lens is clear.
concepts.misconception: The pupil is a black tissue that changes shape to focus light.
concepts.cue: Separate openings, tissues, receptors and neural pathways.
concepts.explanation: The pupil is an opening controlled by the iris; the lens changes shape for fine focus.
sourceRefs: Teacher slides: Anatomy of the Eye & Vision

concepts.definition: the iris changes pupil diameter to regulate how much light enters the eye
concepts.scenario: Moving from a dark room into bright light causes the pupil to become smaller.
concepts.misconception: The pupil itself is a muscle that contracts.
concepts.cue: Identify the muscle and the opening separately.
concepts.explanation: The iris is muscular; the pupil is the opening whose diameter changes.

concepts.definition: the lens changes shape to focus images from different distances on the retina
concepts.scenario: Looking at a nearby phone causes the ciliary muscles to contract and the lens to become rounder.
concepts.misconception: For near vision the ciliary muscles relax and pull the lens flatter.
concepts.cue: Near vision needs a rounder lens and greater refraction.
concepts.explanation: Near: ciliary contraction, reduced ligament tension, rounder lens. Far: the opposite.
sourceRefs: Teacher slides: Anatomy of the Eye & Vision

concepts.definition: nearsightedness in which distant light focuses in front of the retina, commonly corrected with a concave/diverging lens
concepts.scenario: A student can read a book clearly but distant road signs are blurred.
concepts.misconception: Myopia is corrected with a convex lens that converges light more strongly.
sequence: focus forms in front of retina
concepts.cue: Near is clear; far is blurred.
concepts.explanation: A concave/diverging corrective lens moves the distant focal point back onto the retina.
sourceRefs: Teacher slides: Conditions Affecting the Shape of the Eye

concepts.definition: farsightedness in which near light would focus behind the retina, commonly corrected with a convex/converging lens
concepts.scenario: A student sees the board clearly but struggles to focus on nearby print.
concepts.misconception: Hyperopia is caused by light focusing in front of the retina.
concepts.cue: Far is clearer; near is blurred.
concepts.explanation: A convex/converging corrective lens moves the near focal point forward onto the retina.
sourceRefs: Teacher slides: Conditions Affecting the Shape of the Eye

concepts.definition: rods are highly sensitive in dim light and support peripheral/monochrome vision; cones require brighter light and support colour and high acuity
concepts.scenario: At night a faint object may be easier to notice slightly off-centre than by staring directly at it.
concepts.misconception: Rods are concentrated most densely in the fovea and provide sharp colour vision.
concepts.cue: Dim/peripheral points to rods; bright/colour/detail points to cones.
concepts.explanation: Cones are dense at the fovea centralis; rods are more common outside the foveal centre.

concepts.definition: photoreceptors signal to bipolar cells, which signal to ganglion cells; ganglion axons form the optic nerve
concepts.scenario: Light reaches photoreceptors near the choroid even though it first passes through inner retinal neural layers.
concepts.misconception: Ganglion cells are the photoreceptors that directly absorb incoming light.
concepts.cue: Separate the direction of incoming light from the direction of neural output.
concepts.explanation: Light travels inward to rods/cones; neural information then travels photoreceptor → bipolar → ganglion → optic nerve.

concepts.definition: ganglion-cell axons form the optic nerve; fibres partially cross at the optic chiasm and continue toward thalamic relay and occipital visual cortex
concepts.scenario: Damage behind the optic chiasm can affect information from corresponding parts of both visual fields.
concepts.misconception: The optic nerve sends the retinal image directly to the frontal lobe for vision.
concepts.cue: Vision is interpreted in the occipital cortex.
concepts.explanation: The brain integrates visual information after partial crossing and relay; the eye does not itself create perception.

concepts.definition: pinna collects sound; the tympanum vibrates; ossicles amplify; stapes drives the oval window; cochlear fluid motion bends hair cells; auditory nerve carries the signal
concepts.scenario: A sound wave in air becomes mechanical vibration, then fluid movement, then an electrochemical neural signal.
concepts.misconception: Sound waves travel unchanged through the auditory nerve to the brain.
concepts.cue: Track changes in energy form from air pressure to neural signalling.
concepts.explanation: The ear converts and transfers energy; the auditory nerve carries neural impulses, not sound waves.
sourceRefs: Teacher slides: Outer/Middle Ear; Inner Ear

concepts.definition: a passage connecting the middle ear with the throat region that helps equalize air pressure across the tympanum
concepts.scenario: Yawning during an airplane descent can make the ears pop.
concepts.misconception: The Eustachian tube carries sound signals from the cochlea to the brain.
concepts.cue: Think pressure equalization, not hearing transduction.
concepts.explanation: Its major role here is balancing pressure across the eardrum.
sourceRefs: Teacher slides: Parts of Ear not Involved with Hearing

concepts.definition: frequency is perceived mainly as pitch; amplitude is perceived mainly as loudness/intensity
concepts.scenario: A whistle and a tuba differ strongly in frequency, while turning up a speaker mainly changes amplitude.
concepts.misconception: Higher amplitude means a higher pitch.
concepts.cue: How often waves arrive = frequency; how large the pressure variation is = amplitude.
concepts.explanation: Frequency and amplitude are separate wave properties with different perceptual effects.

concepts.definition: conduction loss involves outer/middle-ear sound transfer; sensorineural loss involves hair cells or neural pathways
concepts.scenario: Damaged cochlear stereocilia after repeated loud-noise exposure can cause permanent sensorineural loss.
concepts.misconception: A hearing aid always restores normal hearing regardless of where damage occurs.
concepts.cue: Ask whether sound transfer or sensory/neural transduction is impaired.
concepts.explanation: Amplification may help some conductive deficits, but hair-cell/neural damage is a different problem.

concepts.definition: three fluid-filled canals with hair-cell receptors that detect rotational acceleration of the head
concepts.scenario: After spinning stops, continuing fluid movement can keep bending the cupula and create a false sense of rotation.
concepts.misconception: Otoliths inside the semicircular canals detect all head rotation.
concepts.cue: Rotation belongs to the semicircular canals; otoliths belong to utricle/saccule.
concepts.explanation: Canal fluid movement bends the cupula and receptor hairs, signalling angular acceleration.

concepts.definition: vestibular structures that use otoliths and hair cells to detect head position and linear acceleration relative to gravity
concepts.scenario: Tilting the head shifts otolith mass and bends sensory hairs.
concepts.misconception: The utricle and saccule are the structures that amplify sound through the middle ear.
concepts.cue: Gravity/linear acceleration points to otolith organs.
concepts.explanation: Utricle and saccule complement the rotational sensing of semicircular canals.

concepts.definition: mechanoreceptors in muscles, tendons and joints that provide information about body position and movement
concepts.scenario: With eyes closed, you can still tell whether your elbow is flexed.
concepts.misconception: Body position is detected only by the inner ear.
concepts.cue: Think receptors associated with muscles, tendons and joints.
concepts.explanation: Equilibrium integrates vestibular information with proprioceptive and other sensory input.

concepts.definition: taste receptors respond to dissolved chemicals in the mouth; olfactory receptors respond to airborne odorant molecules in the nasal cavity
concepts.scenario: Pinching the nose can reduce flavour perception because smell contributes strongly to flavour.
concepts.misconception: Taste and smell use mechanoreceptors because food and air physically contact tissues.
concepts.cue: The stimulus is chemical identity, not mechanical pressure.
concepts.explanation: Both systems use chemoreceptors, but in different organs and neural pathways.

concepts.definition: different skin receptors detect touch/pressure, temperature and potentially damaging stimuli; receptor density varies across the body
concepts.scenario: Fingertips can distinguish two nearby touches better than the back because receptor density and receptive-field organization differ.
concepts.misconception: Every square centimetre of skin has the same receptor density and sensitivity.
concepts.cue: Match the receptor to the stimulus type.
concepts.explanation: Skin sensation is a collection of receptor systems, not one universal touch receptor.
sourceRefs: Teacher slides: Receptors in the Skin

authoredQuestions.prompt: Which receptor type is most directly stimulated by light?
authoredQuestions.cue: Match the receptor name to stimulus energy.
authoredQuestions.explanation: Photoreceptors in the retina transduce light energy.

authoredQuestions.prompt: A student stops noticing the hum of a ventilation fan after several minutes. Which process best explains this?
authoredQuestions.cue: The stimulus stayed constant while awareness decreased.
authoredQuestions.explanation: The CNS reduces attention to constant, low-priority sensory input.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes reception from perception?
choices: Reception detects the stimulus; perception interprets sensory information in the brain
Reception occurs in the cortex; perception occurs only in receptors
Perception begins before any receptor is activated
authoredQuestions.answer: Reception detects the stimulus; perception interprets sensory information in the brain
authoredQuestions.cue: Separate detection from interpretation.
authoredQuestions.explanation: Receptors detect/transduce; CNS processing produces perception.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Which structure is the opening through which light enters the inner eye?
authoredQuestions.cue: The opening is not itself a muscle.
authoredQuestions.explanation: The iris controls pupil diameter; the pupil is the opening.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Which sequence correctly traces light after it reaches the front of the eye?
choices: Cornea → pupil → lens → vitreous humour → retina
authoredQuestions.answer: Cornea → pupil → lens → vitreous humour → retina
authoredQuestions.cue: Trace photons to the photoreceptors before thinking about neural output.
authoredQuestions.explanation: The optic nerve carries neural information away after retinal transduction.

authoredQuestions.prompt: A person has a clear cornea and lens but severe damage to the optic nerve. Which outcome is most likely?
choices: Light may reach the retina but visual information cannot be carried normally to the brain
The pupil can no longer admit light
The sclera cannot support the eye
authoredQuestions.answer: Light may reach the retina but visual information cannot be carried normally to the brain
authoredQuestions.cue: Separate optical structures from the neural output pathway.
authoredQuestions.explanation: The optic nerve is required to carry ganglion-cell output toward the brain.

authoredQuestions.prompt: When focusing on a nearby object, what normally happens?
choices: Ciliary muscles contract and the lens becomes rounder
Ciliary muscles relax and the lens becomes rounder
Ciliary muscles contract and the lens becomes flatter
authoredQuestions.answer: Ciliary muscles contract and the lens becomes rounder
authoredQuestions.cue: Near objects require greater refractive power.
authoredQuestions.explanation: Contraction reduces suspensory tension so the elastic lens rounds.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Which correction is paired correctly?
authoredQuestions.cue: Myopia needs the focal point moved farther back.
authoredQuestions.explanation: A concave/diverging lens shifts the distant focal point onto the retina.

authoredQuestions.prompt: A short eyeball causes near images to tend to focus behind the retina. Which condition is described?
authoredQuestions.cue: Think farsightedness.
authoredQuestions.explanation: Hyperopia commonly makes near focusing difficult and is corrected with converging/convex lenses.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Which photoreceptors are most concentrated at the fovea centralis?
authoredQuestions.cue: The fovea supports high-acuity colour vision.
authoredQuestions.explanation: Cone density is highest at the fovea centralis.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Which sequence correctly traces neural information within the retina?
choices: Photoreceptor → bipolar cell → ganglion cell → optic nerve
Ganglion cell → photoreceptor → bipolar cell → optic nerve
Bipolar cell → lens → ganglion cell → optic nerve
Photoreceptor → optic chiasm → bipolar cell → ganglion cell
authoredQuestions.answer: Photoreceptor → bipolar cell → ganglion cell → optic nerve
authoredQuestions.cue: Do not confuse incoming light direction with neural output direction.
authoredQuestions.explanation: Ganglion-cell axons form the optic nerve.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Why is the optic disc called a blind spot?
choices: It lacks photoreceptors where ganglion axons leave the eye
The lens blocks light from reaching it
It has too many cones to distinguish light
authoredQuestions.answer: It lacks photoreceptors where ganglion axons leave the eye
authoredQuestions.cue: Think about where the optic nerve exits.
authoredQuestions.explanation: No rods or cones occupy the optic disc itself.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Which structure receives vibration directly from the stapes?
authoredQuestions.cue: This boundary transfers ossicle motion into inner-ear fluid pressure waves.
authoredQuestions.explanation: The stapes footplate acts at the oval window.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Where does mechanical sound energy become receptor-based neural signalling?
choices: Hair cells of the organ of Corti
authoredQuestions.answer: Hair cells of the organ of Corti
authoredQuestions.cue: Look for mechanoreceptors.
authoredQuestions.explanation: Bending stereocilia changes hair-cell signalling to auditory nerve fibres.

authoredQuestions.prompt: What is the main role of the Eustachian tube in this chapter?
authoredQuestions.cue: Think of ears popping during altitude changes.
authoredQuestions.explanation: Opening the tube permits pressure equilibration with the throat region.

authoredQuestions.prompt: A higher-frequency sound is generally perceived as what?
authoredQuestions.cue: Frequency and amplitude are different wave properties.
authoredQuestions.explanation: Frequency mainly corresponds to perceived pitch.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Repeated loud-noise exposure permanently damages cochlear stereocilia. Which category best fits the resulting loss?
authoredQuestions.cue: The damage is at sensory hair cells.
authoredQuestions.explanation: Hair-cell damage impairs transduction and is not simply a sound-conduction problem.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Which structure is most directly associated with rotational acceleration?
authoredQuestions.cue: Three loops are arranged in three spatial planes.
authoredQuestions.explanation: Fluid movement bends cupula-associated hair cells during head rotation.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Which statement correctly places otoliths?
choices: They act with hair cells in the utricle and saccule
They sit in the middle-ear ossicles
authoredQuestions.answer: They act with hair cells in the utricle and saccule
authoredQuestions.cue: Otolith organs detect gravity/linear acceleration.
authoredQuestions.explanation: Do not place otoliths in the semicircular canals.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Which receptor class is used by taste and smell?
authoredQuestions.cue: The relevant stimulus is a chemical molecule.
authoredQuestions.explanation: Taste and olfaction both depend on chemical binding to receptors.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Why can fingertips discriminate fine touch better than many areas of the back?
choices: They have denser touch receptor representation and smaller receptive fields
They connect directly to the optic nerve
authoredQuestions.answer: They have denser touch receptor representation and smaller receptive fields
authoredQuestions.cue: Compare receptor density, not skin thickness alone.
authoredQuestions.explanation: Higher receptor density supports finer spatial discrimination.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Which statement correctly follows a visual signal from environmental stimulus to perception?
choices: Light → photoreceptor transduction → bipolar/ganglion signalling → optic nerve → visual cortex
Light → optic nerve → lens → rods → cerebellum
Light → Eustachian tube → retina → temporal lobe
Light → iris → auditory nerve → visual cortex
authoredQuestions.answer: Light → photoreceptor transduction → bipolar/ganglion signalling → optic nerve → visual cortex
authoredQuestions.cue: Separate optical input from neural output.
authoredQuestions.explanation: The final perception depends on cortical processing of retinal neural output.

authoredQuestions.prompt: A person can detect vibration at the tympanum but has destroyed cochlear hair cells. Which step fails most directly?
choices: Transduction of cochlear mechanical movement into sensory neural signalling
Collection of sound by the pinna
Pressure equalization through the Eustachian tube
authoredQuestions.answer: Transduction of cochlear mechanical movement into sensory neural signalling
authoredQuestions.cue: Hair cells are the receptors.
authoredQuestions.explanation: Mechanical transmission may still occur, but receptor conversion is impaired.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Explain why a person with myopia can often see nearby objects more clearly than distant objects, and identify the corrective lens used.
answerKey: Distant light focuses in front of the retina
Correction shifts the focus onto the retina
authoredQuestions.explanation: A complete answer connects eyeball/focal geometry to the lens correction.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Trace both the direction of incoming light through the retina and the direction of neural signalling after photoreceptors respond.
answerKey: Light passes through ganglion/bipolar layers toward rods and cones
Bipolar cells transmit toward ganglion cells
authoredQuestions.explanation: This explicitly corrects the common direction-reversal misconception.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Trace the major structures that transfer sound energy from the outer ear to the auditory nerve.
authoredQuestions.explanation: The answer should also acknowledge the conversion from mechanical energy to neural signalling.

authoredQuestions.prompt: Compare how the semicircular canals and the utricle/saccule contribute to equilibrium.
answerKey: Semicircular canals detect rotational acceleration via fluid/cupula/hair cells
Utricle and saccule detect gravity/linear acceleration via otoliths/hair cells
Both send vestibular sensory information to the CNS
authoredQuestions.explanation: Otoliths must not be assigned to the semicircular canals.

authoredQuestions.prompt: A student says, 'The eye sees an image and sends the finished picture to the brain.' Correct the statement using at least three biological structures or processes.
answerKey: Brain/occipital cortex integrates and perceives visual information
authoredQuestions.explanation: The eye provides optical focusing and retinal transduction; conscious perception is a brain process.

generatorGuidance.multipleChoice: Use authoredQuestions directly first. Additional MC may be generated from concept fields only when distractors are plausible within the same topic.
